name: The no historical data problem
blurb: How actuaries price a novel exposure without decades of claims to reason from.
summary: How actuaries price a novel exposure without decades of claims to reason from.

part_3_high_value_red_flags: A blanket exclusion for any loss arising out of artificial intelligence, machine learning, or algorithmic decision making, which would eliminate most core coverage.
A cyber liability sublimit that caps data breach and privacy claims at a fraction of the primary limit, leaving the insured exposed to class action costs.
A professional services exclusion that removes coverage for erroneous AI predictions or advice provided to customers.
A failure to perform exclusion that bars claims for the AI system not meeting contractual accuracy, uptime, or output specifications.
A bodily injury exclusion for autonomous vehicles, robotics, or medical devices that use the AI, which would defeat product liability coverage.
A data loss or data restoration exclusion that denies first party costs to rebuild corrupted training data or customer databases.
A prior acts or known loss exclusion that excludes any defect or vulnerability discovered before policy inception, even if no claim has been reported.
manuscript_wording_and_carve_backs: Negotiate removal of the blanket artificial intelligence exclusion and replace it with a narrow exclusion only for intentional misuse or unapproved modification of the AI system.
Add an affirmative endorsement covering third party liability arising from algorithmic discrimination, subject to a sublimit and a requirement that the insured has implemented bias testing.
Amend the definition of occurrence to include continuous or repeated exposure to substantially the same general harmful conditions, so that latent AI defects are not split into multiple deductibles.
Add a data restoration endorsement that covers the cost to recreate, restore, or recollect corrupted training data and customer data up to a specified sublimit.
Remove the professional services exclusion for AI generated advice and replace it with a professional liability sublimit that applies only to claims alleging negligent design or failure to warn.
Add contingent business interruption coverage for loss of income due to failure of a named cloud service provider or power utility, with a waiting period of no more than twelve hours.
Carve back the failure to perform exclusion to allow coverage for sudden and accidental failure of the AI system, while excluding gradual degradation or expected performance shortfalls.

part_4_program_structure_and_limits.bi_waiting_period: Business interruption waiting periods for data centre operations are typically twenty four to seventy two hours, but underwriters may impose a longer waiting period of seven days for novel AI dependent revenue streams where loss quantification is uncertain.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.business_interruption: Business interruption coverage is often sublimited to a percentage of the property limit, commonly twenty five to fifty percent, and may exclude contingent losses from cloud provider outages unless specifically endorsed.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.property_eb_equipment: Electronic data processing equipment is usually written on a separate schedule with a sublimit for replacement cost, often capped at five million to ten million dollars per location, because underwriters cannot rely on historical failure rates for novel cooling or power systems.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.per_occurrence_primary_excess_layered_pr: Property coverage for data centre buildings and contents is placed on a layered basis with a primary layer typically covering the first ten million to twenty five million dollars of physical damage, and excess layers stacked above that based on modelled catastrophe scenarios.

part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.cgl_primary: Primary commercial general liability limits are typically low, often one million to two million dollars per occurrence, because underwriters treat the novel exposure as unproven and seek to cap first layer severity.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.paper_basis: Claims made basis applies here because the manifestation of AI defects or data centre failures may occur years after the policy period, and underwriters need a fixed reporting window to manage the absence of historical claims data.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.excess_umbrella_towers: Excess and umbrella towers are layered in small increments, often five million to ten million dollars per layer, with each layer priced on a modelled frequency severity curve rather than historical loss development.

part_1_core_third_party_liability_exposu: Bodily injury or property damage caused by an autonomous decision made by the AI system without human intervention.
Personal and advertising injury from algorithmic discrimination, defamation, or false arrest generated by the model output.
Intellectual property infringement from training data or generated content that reproduces copyrighted material.
Failure to perform a contractual obligation where the AI system fails to meet a specified accuracy or uptime standard.
Data breach or privacy violation arising from the AI system's collection, processing, or leakage of personal data.
Professional liability for erroneous advice or predictions provided by the AI to end users.
Product liability for a physical device incorporating the AI that malfunctions and causes harm.

underwriter_wants_to_know: What is the specific novel AI application and its potential failure modes that lack historical claims data.
How the insured's model validation, testing, and monitoring procedures substitute for actuarial loss history.
What third party data sources or analogous industry loss data the broker can provide to benchmark frequency and severity.
Whether the insured has any contractual liability allocations or indemnities that shift risk away from the insurer.
What the insured's incident response and post market surveillance capabilities are for detecting latent defects.
How the insured quantifies tail risk from rare but severe events like model collapse or data centre cascading failure.
What regulatory or litigation trends exist for similar AI exposures in other jurisdictions.
